summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a United States commonwealth, and national law governs travel documents, immigration and entry screening there. The commonwealth's own code governs hate-crime sentencing, marriage, adoption, gender-marker change and public-employment discrimination, and those are the areas where a trans visitor or resident meets territory-level rules rather than national ones.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the Northern Mariana Islands. Marriage between two people of the same sex has been recognised since 2015, following the United States Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges; the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015, and adoption has been available since the same year.

Legal change of gender marker is permitted, but only where the applicant has completed a specified medical process set out in commonwealth law.

The commonwealth has no comprehensive nondiscrimination statute of its own.

A 2023 amendment to the Commonwealth Code, Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, sets criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants convicted of hate-motivated crimes, and the hate-crimes statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
An external policy index scoring the Northern Mariana Islands as of 27 September 2026 records a sexual orientation policy score of 3.5 out of 22, a gender identity policy score of minus 2 out of 25, and an overall score of 1.5 out of 47, each in the low or negative band. The negative gender identity score reflects an index methodology in which restrictive measures are counted as outweighing protective ones.

The same index records full marriage recognition since 2015 while recording no comprehensive nondiscrimination coverage, so the territory's protection varies by area of law.
localsOnly:
Commonwealth-level discrimination protections extend to government employees only; other recourse runs through federal employment-discrimination law.

The territory's first Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan, on Saipan, with about 60 people attending.
outOfScopeNotes:
Public Law 22-32 sets criteria for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes; no record of prosecutions, convictions or sentences imposed under it was identified, so its effect in practice is not established.

The policy index scores are an assessment of written policy as of 27 September 2026 and do not measure enforcement, policing practice or day-to-day treatment.

The medical process required for legal gender change is not itemised in the available sources; the specific requirements are unresolved.

No commonwealth-specific data on trans-targeted violence, police conduct, or access to sex-segregated facilities was identified.
